definition: Epistemic modal logic is a subfield of modal logic that is concerned with reasoning about knowledge.
details: While epistemology has a long philosophical tradition dating back to Ancient Greece, epistemic logic is a much more recent development with applications in many fields, including philosophy, theoretical computer science, artificial intelligence, economics, and linguistics. While philosophers since Aristotle have discussed modal logic, and Medieval philosophers such as Avicenna, Ockham, and Duns Scotus developed many of their observations, it was C. I. Lewis who created the first symbolic and systematic approach to the topic, in 1912. It continued to mature as a field, reaching its modern form in 1963 with the work of Saul Kripke.

explainer.lead: Epistemic modal logic gives us a precise way to talk about knowledge, not just facts. It helps distinguish what is true from what a particular person or agent knows, which matters in philosophy, artificial intelligence, computer science, economics, and linguistics.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a toy is hidden in a box: the toy being there is one thing, but you knowing it is there is another. This kind of logic uses special statements to keep those ideas separate, so we can reason carefully about who knows what.
tiers.practitioner: Use it when an AI or computer-science model must distinguish the state of the world from an agent's knowledge of that state. A common pitfall is treating a true proposition as automatically known, or treating one agent's knowledge as shared by every agent.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text notation, K_a p means that agent a knows proposition p, so p and K_a p are distinct claims; expressions such as K_a K_b p can represent knowledge about another agent's knowledge. C. I. Lewis introduced the first symbolic, systematic approach to modal logic in 1912, and Saul Kripke's work brought it to its modern form in 1963.

explainer.example: Suppose the key is in a drawer and Alice has seen it there, but Bob has not. The logic can express “the key is in the drawer,” “Alice knows the key is in the drawer,” and “Bob does not know that Alice knows where the key is” as separate claims.

usedIn.detail: It connects formal modal reasoning with questions about knowledge.

explainer.intuition: A fact can be true without anyone knowing it, and different agents can know different things. Epistemic modal logic adds knowledge to modal reasoning so those distinctions can be expressed and examined formally.
howItWorks: Start with ordinary propositions about facts.
Name the agent whose knowledge is being described.
Use a knowledge statement such as “Alice knows p.”
Keep that statement separate from the claim that p is true.
Combine statements to reason about knowledge of knowledge.
explainer.whyItMatters: It turns informal questions about who knows what into precise statements that can be analysed systematically. That makes it useful across fields where knowledge, rather than truth alone, affects reasoning.
misconceptions: It is not the whole philosophical study of knowledge.
A proposition being true does not mean an agent knows it.
Different agents need not have the same knowledge.
